workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§121–124
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§121–124: Qorchi's Omen and the Making of Chinggis Qahan
part: §§121–124 — Qorchi's Omen and the Making of Chinggis Qahan
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§121–124, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Four sections. §121 is Qorchi's speech to Temüjin: he and Jamuqa are of one birth, and a vision of a hornless ox and a cow, the cow butting Jamuqa and the ox bringing the realm, tells him that Heaven and Earth have chosen Temüjin; he asks for ten thousand men and thirty wives. §122 lists the clans that leave Jamuqa and join Temüjin at Ail-Qaraqana, and the move to the Kökö-Na'ur. §123 has Altan, Quchar and Sacha-Beki offer to make Temüjin Qan, with the vows they swear; he is named Chinggis Qahan. §124 is the first distribution of duties among his companions: quivers, cooks, shepherds, cart-keepers, swordsmen, horse-herds, arrows, and Sübegetei's vow to serve as mouse, crow and felt. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.i: We were born of the woman whom Bodonchar-Boqdo seized and took, and with Jamuqa we were of one belly and a single afterbirth.
sentences.n: Qorchi claims kinship with Jamuqa: both come from the woman Bodončar seized (barižu abuγsan, Ming 拿着 要了的, 'seizing, taking'). The two ba differ: the first (Ming 也) is 'and, also'; the one after büleġei (Ming 俺) is 'we', placed after the verb as the glossary has it. keke is Ming 胞漿, which I read as afterbirth; nigeten and γaγčatan carry the plural possessive -ten/-tan ('those having one belly, those having a single afterbirth', Ming (有的)每). I take the whole as a literal claim of shared birth, but it could be figurative. Long sentence broken at büleġei ba; it runs on to the next unit, which Shiratori closes with his full stop.

sentences.i: "Temüjin, if you become lord of the realm, how will you make me glad, since I have told of it?" he said.
sentences.n: The quotation inside the speech: Qorchi asks for his reward. nama-ji žiγ̇aγsan-u tula is 'on account of having told', with nama-ji 'me' as the one to be made glad; the teller is Qorchi himself, who calls himself 'the man who told' in his next speech. The Ming prints 吉了 的 for žiγ̇aγsan-u, where the same word is 吿 'tell' elsewhere, so 吉 is probably a copyist's slip. žirγaγ̇ulqu is 'to make glad' (敎快活).
